Denise, you have twenty minutes with the board and twenty-six slides. Something has to go. Tell me the through-line first.
The growth is real, and it has bought us a risk we have not priced.
Good. That is one sentence and I can repeat it. Now, what is the build?
Three steps. What drove the quarter was the corporate portfolio. What it cost us was capacity in the south. And what it exposes us to is one bad season.
Three slides, then. What are the other twenty-three doing?
Nine of them are market granularity. They are good slides, and they answer questions nobody in that room is going to ask.
So put them in the appendix and stop mourning them. What about the broker analysis? That one I like.
I like it too, and it goes to the back as well. It does not serve the through-line. It tees up a different presentation, and that one is for November.
That is the first time I have heard you cut something you were proud of. Send me the four slides tonight.
What it cost us was capacity in the south.

I rebuild board decks for a living, and I only ever ask one question about a slide. Does it serve the through-line? If it does, it stays. If it does not, it goes to the appendix. That is the whole method, and it is harder than it sounds, because the slides that fail the test are usually good slides. The appendix is what makes this possible at all. Nobody can cut when cutting means losing the work. Move it to the back and the work is still there, still yours, still available when somebody asks. It is simply no longer standing between the room and the decision. And the hardest slide to cut is always the one you are proudest of. That is not a coincidence. You are proud of it because it took you three days, and three days of your work is not the same thing as three minutes of the board's attention. One more thing. A deck with no through-line makes the room do the work of finding the point, and a room that has to do that stops trying somewhere around slide six.

For years I believed that presenting in another language meant compensating. If my English was going to be simpler than my own language, then I had better use more of it, so that nobody thought the ideas underneath were simple too. It took an unkind colleague to show me what was actually happening. The extra words were not protecting the ideas, they were burying them, and the room was reading the length as uncertainty. Now I do something almost mechanical. I write the fact. Then I ask myself, out loud, so what? And whatever answers that question is the sentence that goes on the slide. The fact itself goes underneath, in small type, for anybody who wants it. The strange part, and it still surprises me, is that the sentences that survive are shorter than anything I would write in my own language. And they land harder. It turns out that a second language does not make you simpler. It just removes your ability to hide.

The growth is real, and it has bought us a risk we have not priced. What drove the quarter was the corporate portfolio. What it exposes us to is one bad season. What I need from you today is a decision on the limits.
